news.summary_zh: 英伟达CEO黄仁勋被指以羞辱作为激励手段，应对员工因公司股价上涨获得财务自由后的动力缺失问题
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】黄仁勋（英伟达创始人兼CEO）在英伟达内部管理层会议：通过羞辱下属以取代传统财务激励，试图维持员工在高薪状态下的工作压力与输出效能
【起因与机理】因员工财富快速积累导致传统绩效激励失效，试图寻找新的替代性驱动机制
【核心事实细节】黄仁勋被指以羞辱作为应对高薪员工动力缺失的核心手段。
【各方立场与态度】该管理风格可能导致高端技术人才流失，削弱公司的长期技术研发护城河。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Jensen Huang, Founder and CEO of Nvidia: Using public humiliation to replace traditional financial incentives to maintain employee work intensity and performance output
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Traditional performance-based incentives have lost efficacy due to the rapid wealth accumulation of employees
[Key Metrics] Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Such management styles risk talent attrition, potentially weakening the company's long-term R&D moat.
paragraphs: As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.
“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.

Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.

Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Mr. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Mr. Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Mr. Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Mr. Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)

Mr. Huang denied Mr. Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Mr. Fisher said. Mr. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Mr. Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Mr. Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Mr. Huang.

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.

Mr. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.

Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Mr. Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Mr. Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
But in the eyes of some, Mr. Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.

In September 2004, Mr. Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Mr. Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H.R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Mr. Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.
In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.
That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Mr. Huang said at one point.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”

Mr. Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”

Mr. Winston said he then confronted Mr. Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

That November, Mr. Winston was called into a meeting with Mr. Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Mr. Huang told Mr. Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Mr. Winston sued Nvidia, Mr. Huang said he would make sure Mr. Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.
“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Mr. Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”

In the months that followed, Mr. Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Mr. Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Mr. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Mr. Huang.
But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.
Mr. Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.

In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Mr. Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Mr. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”

Mr. Pettigrew discussed Mr. Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Mr. Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Mr. Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.

Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Mr. Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.

After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Mr. Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A.I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.
“You’re not even speaking human,” Mr. Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

paragraphs: As Nvidia became wealthier and wealthier in recent years, Jensen Huang grew increasingly frustrated with his staff.

He told groups of subordinates that they had become so rich that he couldn’t motivate them simply with money, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential conversations. The only way he could grind more work out of them, he added, was through humiliation.

This was an extension of a philosophy that went back decades. Mr. Huang had for years been berating his employees, documents and interviews show. His tongue lashings were savage and inventive. He told one executive that his mother should have aborted him, according to one witness. He said he would rip both arms off a subordinate and beat the person over the head to death with them. And he told another employee he would rip off the top of their head and “pee on your brain.”

The tirades were a centerpiece of the culture at Nvidia throughout its meteoric rise to a $5 trillion company and cornerstone of the artificial intelligence revolution. They were also foundational to Mr. Huang’s management style.
“I’d rather torture you into greatness, because I believe in you,” he once said.

He has long used humiliation as a tool, excoriating employees in front of their peers with insults, personal attacks and violent comments, while telling them it was good for them or for the business, according to more than a dozen current and former employees, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal, and to a review of hundreds of pages of court records and other documents spanning more than 20 years. The behavior kept Nvidia’s human resources department busy fielding workplace complaints, but some employees said the department did not take them seriously.

Mr. Huang also inspired love and reverence from many of his employees. Thousands have signed a letter asking for his return. Some have tattoos of Nvidia’s logo. Both those who liked Mr. Huang and those who disliked him described Nvidia as cultish. He cultivated loyalty through not just his technical mastery but also acts of personal compassion and praise. But he ruled through fear.

Mr. Huang’s behavior began long before Nvidia became one of the most valuable companies in the world. In at least two cases originating in the mid-2000s, the company struck settlements with former senior leaders, both of whom had raised concerns about Mr. Huang’s conduct, saying it was unlawful and exposed Nvidia to liability.

Michael Winston, a former senior vice president of human resources, threatened to sue Nvidia in 2005, saying that he had been fired after objecting to Mr. Huang’s conduct, which he described as “the most verbally abusive, threatening and intimidating behavior” he had witnessed in his career. Mr. Huang “thinks he can get away with anything,” Mr. Winston wrote in notes he made around that time, which were reviewed by The New York Times.
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Mr. Winston for more than $1 million, which has not been previously reported.

Mr. Huang resigned from Nvidia last week, after revelations of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom U.S. intelligence believes to be a Chinese intelligence asset. But his imprint remains on the culture of the company he co-founded in 1993.

Some managers followed Mr. Huang’s lead, six current and former employees said — including his own daughter, Madison, who as his de facto chief of staff often yelled at people, including executives senior to her. (She continues to work at Nvidia.)

Mr. Huang denied Mr. Winston’s allegations in a statement from his spokesman, John Fisher, saying they are from an employee who was fired. They are “fabrications that are now impossible to disprove specifically, and the thousands of Nvidia employees who continue to speak out for Jensen show they’re false,” Mr. Fisher said. Mr. Fisher declined to answer other questions regarding Mr. Huang’s behavior.

Nvidia declined to comment. Its board and Colette Kress, its interim chief executive, must now decide if the company will continue in the mold of Mr. Huang or forge a new way forward. She will do so in the face of pressure from Mr. Huang and his supporters, who are agitating for his return to the company. Mr. Huang once belittled Ms. Kress in a meeting with top executives, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Harvey C. Jones, the chair of Nvidia’s board, said Tuesday that it “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as C.E.O.” Earlier this month, the board opened an investigation into Mr. Huang.

Silicon Valley has a long history of founders and chief executives with caustic management styles. Steve Jobs, the co-founder and chief executive of Apple, was infamous for screaming at and insulting employees who did not meet his exacting standards. He was also beloved. Employees credited his approach with helping to create culture-changing products like the iPod and iPhone.

Mr. Huang had a similar effect on his staff. He created a flat organizational structure where he interacted with employees at almost every level of the business. He impressed them with his vision for the future of technology, his command of business strategy and the speed at which he tackled and seemed to conquer new areas of importance, leading the company to the forefront of the A.I. boom.

Many of the company’s senior leaders have worked for Mr. Huang for more than a decade. Some shared Mr. Huang’s belief that mediocrity should be stamped out and excellence pursued, said four current and former employees. If employees didn’t like it, they could leave.
But in the eyes of some, Mr. Huang’s behavior was extreme, even by Silicon Valley standards.

In September 2004, Mr. Winston joined Nvidia to lead human resources. A longtime human resources executive who previously worked at Merrill Lynch and Motorola, Mr. Winston was soon taken aback by the disarray of the H.R. department and the cultural norms of Nvidia. This account of his time at the company is based on interviews and Mr. Winston’s notes and emails, as well as drafts of a lawsuit and other legal documents reviewed by The Times.
In his first days at Nvidia, he learned that two key human resources leaders had just quit and others were on the verge of resigning.
That October, at a two-day off-site meeting attended by about 50 employees, Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang unleashed graphic violent threats.
“You have to do this, or I will rip your fucking heart out and stomp on it,” Mr. Huang said at one point.

“I watched them helpless, as they were publicly humiliated, indeed tormented, for extended periods of time, by this lunatic!” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “It pained me physically, intellectually and emotionally to be in the room.”

Mr. Winston said other attendees were “terrorized” and pleaded with him to intervene. Days later, he voiced his concerns during a meeting with top executives. One told him that the conduct was typical but could be a liability for the company. Another advised him to “toughen up.”

Mr. Winston said he then confronted Mr. Huang, warning him that he had “crossed the line” and that mistreating employees could expose Nvidia to lawsuits. He said Mr. Huang dismissed the concerns and defended public humiliation as a “rite of passage.” Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang bragged to him that he subjected new employees to it during their first six months at the company to test whether they would stand for it.
Mr. Winston said Mr. Huang told him that he would not stop. “It has good entertainment value,” Mr. Huang told him.

That November, Mr. Winston was called into a meeting with Mr. Huang and another executive, who then fired him. Mr. Huang told Mr. Winston that he was “not a good fit.” If Mr. Winston sued Nvidia, Mr. Huang said he would make sure Mr. Winston never worked in Silicon Valley again.
“To say Nvidia fired me because it just was not ‘a fit’ is nothing more than a smokescreen,” Mr. Winston said in his notes. “The real issue,” he wrote, was Mr. Huang’s “unconscionable behavior.”

In the months that followed, Mr. Winston filed a formal complaint against Nvidia with California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing, making allegations that he was fired for opposing Mr. Huang’s treatment of employees, including what he said constituted sexual harassment. Mr. Winston then drafted a lawsuit against Nvidia and Mr. Huang.
But before the complaint was filed, both sides reached a settlement. Neither side admitted liability or wrongdoing.
Mr. Winston rejoined the banking industry, and later blew the whistle against Countrywide Financial Corporation for its conduct during the buildup to the financial crisis. He died earlier this year.

In 2007, Stephen Pettigrew, a former lawyer for the company, sued Nvidia over claims that included age discrimination and retaliation for reporting Mr. Winston’s allegations of sexual harassment. Mr. Pettigrew reported in a complaint filed with the California Department of Fair Employment and Housing that he sought “emergency medical attention for severe nervous tension and anxiety, as a direct result of the actions of Nvidia.”

Mr. Pettigrew discussed Mr. Winston’s complaint during depositions for his own lawsuit, citing Mr. Winston’s allegations as evidence of misconduct that exposed Nvidia to legal risk. Nvidia’s general counsel at the time, David Shannon, confirmed during another deposition in the case that Mr. Winston’s dispute was resolved in a pre-litigation financial settlement.

Nvidia denied all wrongdoing, and said that Mr. Pettigrew was fired for poor performance. The company countersued, saying that he breached his contract and misused company documents. The case ultimately settled out of court in 2009.

After Nvidia’s chips were used in 2012 to train an early artificial intelligence system, Mr. Huang concluded that the future of computing would be A.I. Employees recall receiving his email on a Friday saying the company was pivoting its business from graphics to deep learning, a precursor to A.I. He froze hiring for anybody but experts in that field, and Nvidia became an A.I. chipmaker overnight.

A decade later, Mr. Huang’s bet paid off when ChatGPT arrived, kick-starting frenzied interest and investment in A.I. Demand for Nvidia’s chips skyrocketed, and the company’s value soared. Many of the company’s 42,000 employees became fabulously wealthy and were exhilarated to be at the forefront of a technology Mr. Huang referred to as the next Industrial Revolution.

In the wake of Mr. Huang’s resignation, some employees have shared stories of a boss who went out of his way to support them. Last week, Vartika Singh, who works on strategy at Nvidia, recalled Mr. Huang’s support when her sister had brain cancer.

“Thank you, Jensen,” Ms. Singh wrote in a social media post. “For your guidance, for believing in people and ideas long before the rest of us understood them, and above all, for your extraordinary humanity.”

Mr. Huang’s mix of disparagement and motivation created something akin to Stockholm syndrome, six current and former employees said. The phenomenon, in which somebody held captive develops an emotional bond with their abuser, mirrored their relationship with Mr. Huang, they said.

Rather than fire people, Mr. Huang sometimes preferred to further humiliate them. When Ned Finkle, his former vice president of strategic marketing, faltered in a meeting with a major customer, Mr. Huang chewed him out in front of executives from the other company, said two people who spoke anonymously about the private exchange.

Mr. Huang then named Mr. Finkle vice president of external affairs, or government relations. At the time, Mr. Huang considered it one of the least important jobs at Nvidia, the two people said. Mr. Finkle did not respond to requests for comment.
Mr. Huang’s tirades continued until the end.

He usually did not meet one-on-one with subordinates because, he has publicly said, such meetings reduced transparency within Nvidia. But top executives considered the move a power play that gave Mr. Huang more control. If anyone disagreed with Mr. Huang, they would have to do so in front of a group. Mr. Huang could then fire back, ridiculing that person in front of everyone else.
Mr. Huang also ripped into longtime leaders in front of their own teams, telling them their boss was incompetent and unqualified, two people said.

In one instance, Mr. Huang went around a room, telling managers he would kill them, according to one person with knowledge of the incident. When he reached a person in their 70s, Mr. Huang said that the person was really old and everyone hoped they would drop dead.

Mr. Huang also made personal attacks. He once made fun of an executive who had taken his children camping and said he needed to find a more committed employee for the job, according to one person. He often mocked another executive for enjoying aviation as a hobby, two people said.

In 2019, after Nvidia lost a bid to help build a U.S. government supercomputer, Mr. Huang castigated a sales executive in front of government officials for missing out on part of a contract worth hundreds of millions of dollars. The executive then threw his employee badge at Mr. Huang, who said he accepted the executive’s resignation on the spot, according to two people with knowledge of the incident.

Mr. Huang’s behavior rubbed off on other senior leaders at the company, including his daughter, Madison. On one call last year with Nvidia’s marketing team, Ms. Huang repeatedly berated a vice president, who then left the call, according to a recording of the meeting reviewed by The Times.
“I’m having an anxiety attack,” the vice president said. “I’m going to drop off. I’m sorry.”
Ms. Huang did not respond to requests for comment.

As Nvidia became the linchpin of the A.I. boom, Mr. Huang’s conduct started to spill outside the company. At Nvidia’s developer conference earlier this year, Mr. Huang moderated a panel with business partners, including Arthur Mensch, the chief executive of the French A.I. start-up Mistral.
During the panel, Mr. Huang interrupted Mr. Mensch several times, apparently taking issue with the Mistral chief executive’s French accent, according to two people who watched the talk.
“You’re not even speaking human,” Mr. Huang said at one point, before another panelist intervened. A spokesman for Mistral declined to comment.
Daniel Gutierrez, an A.I. researcher and longtime “Jensen fan” who was watching the panel, said the interaction changed his perspective on Mr. Huang.

“I thought in the moment, what is happening right now that’s causing you to attack this poor guy?” Mr. Gutierrez said. “When all the new stuff happened in the last week, I go, wait a minute now. Maybe Jensen isn’t the guy I thought I revered.”

news.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
news.title_en: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
news.author: Jess Weatherbed
news.content_snippet: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents
news.summary_en: Meredith Whittaker, President of Signal, announced that integrated OS-level AI agents undermine app-level privacy. To mitigate this, Signal has disabled screenshot functionality on iOS and Android to prevent AI assistants from harvesting encrypted message data, while demanding that OS providers implement transparent technical controls for developer-side AI access management.
paragraphs: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device filesystem.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

news.title_en: Muse Is Unleashing a World of Pettiness on Instagram
news.author: Jason Parham
news.content_snippet:

news.summary_en: Meta's AI assistant Muse is being widely utilized by users to execute automated, bulk unfollow operations. The tool accurately identifies non-reciprocal followers and generates detailed category lists, while mitigating the risk of account suspension typically associated with third-party automated scripts.
paragraphs: Khalil Roberts had heard horror stories of people getting kicked off Instagram for using third-party apps to purge follower counts, so when he came across an X post claiming that Muse—Meta’s AI assistant—could mass-unfollow people who didn’t follow him back, he didn’t believe it.

“I’ve never gone through my exact list to vet those people out, but I’ve always been curious,” the 31-year-old New Yorker tells WIRED. But after realizing that by using Muse, his account wouldn’t get flagged as spam, his mind was made up. “I was like, I actually will be a little petty.”

After downloading Muse, Roberts, who had over 7,600 followers, entered the prompt: “Can you show me a list of people (non celebrity) that [don’t] follow me back on instagram and can you unfollow them for me. ”

Within minutes, Muse identified 151 accounts. It attached an Excel sheet with a breakdown of everyone cataloged—separated by categories identifying their username, real name, classification, and profile link—and asked if Roberts wanted to proceed with his request. Shockingly, some of the names were people he thought of as friends. “It was a little surprising, but also a reminder that we don’t have a relationship anymore.”

Following the success of his November 7 cleanse, Roberts posted about it on X, offering instructions to his followers. Over the past several weeks, parallel scenarios have played out across X, Instagram, and Facebook, with users sharing tips on how to automate their unfollows with the help of Muse.

X user @justdrmj posted about the trend the same week as Roberts, and nearly every reply shared a taste for trivial grudge-holding. For him it came down to one simple rule: “Why be a fan?” “i agree. reciprocity is key,” one person said in response. “The way I just cleaned house,” added another. In a seeming outburst of celebration, one X user posted: “Just unfollowed 1000+ people on IG.”

Even tech worker Kimberly Munoz, who has 33,200 Instagram followers, said she wasn’t about to be “anybody’s fan,” noting in an Instagram video that she used the feature to suss out “people that I know in real life that have unfollowed me.” “I downloaded Muse just to do this only,” one person responded.

With social media rapidly evolving, there is no longer a unified consensus around etiquette. For some people, following others is an indication of friendship or simply a way to keep tabs on your latest crush. Others view it as more of a social obligation—you follow someone if they follow you, but the opposite is true as well.

Natalie Pennington, an associate professor who researches social connection at Colorado State University, wonders about the consequences of people gradually outsourcing small social decisions to technology.

“It is probably at least partially a question of not wanting to deal with emotionally uncomfortable things,” Pennington says. “This also strikes me as another example of information we don’t really need that social media can give us. There’s this data that exists at the platform level or would take a lot of effort to find out on your own, but now you can learn with the click of the button. But it doesn’t mean it is something you need to know.”

In October, despite the seeming popularity of the feature, Meta removed an advertising campaign that promoted Muse with the promise that users could “see who unfollowed you each week,” Business Insider reported.
When WIRED asked about the reasoning behind Meta’s decision to remove the ad, the company did not respond to a request for comment.
But Muse’s capabilities aren’t just being employed to even scores. Some people are using the assistant to streamline feeds that have become extremely cluttered over the years.

Elizabeth Brooks is a self-proclaimed “sweeper”—the term for a hobbyist who routinely enters sweepstakes and promotional contests—who, over the course of 10 years, had followed various accounts offering giveaways. Recently, she started prompting the assistant to bring her five profile links every few hours, no more than six times a day, for her to manually unfollow one by one. “Your following list can finally work for you instead of the other way around,” she wrote on Facebook.

Roberts, who joined Instagram in high school 15 years ago and calls the platform “my app of choice,” says people are becoming more intentional about their digital relationships and who they let into their online lives. But he doesn’t plan on letting Muse make any more decisions about his social life, he says.
“Unfollowing is where I draw the line.”

paragraphs: AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here.

China’s securities regulator has told some law firms it will not approve plans by red-chip companies to list outside mainland China, people familiar with the matter said. The move marks a further tightening of China’s controls on offshore fundraising and will deal a blow to Hong Kong’s initial public offering (IPO) market.
Red-chip companies are incorporated outside China and legally classified as foreign companies, but hold assets and operate businesses within China through equity holdings or contractual arrangements.

Reuters reported on Friday (20 November), citing people familiar with the matter, that the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) recently told representatives of law firms that red-chip companies established after new offshore listing rules took effect in 2023 must move their place of incorporation back to China before they can list.

In March 2023, the CSRC introduced new filing rules for overseas securities offerings and listings by domestic companies, bringing both direct and indirect overseas listings under a filing-based regulatory framework.
Before that, Chinese companies did not need regulatory approval to raise funds overseas through offshore holding structures.
In March this year, the CSRC told Reuters it was reviewing the “necessity and compliance” of red-chip structures.

However, despite warnings from the authorities, some red-chip companies seeking IPOs and their advisers continued to seek regulatory approval, hoping to list outside mainland China without dismantling their existing structures or moving their place of incorporation back to China, according to one of the people familiar with the matter.
The person added that most applicants had failed to convince Chinese regulators that their red-chip structures were necessary, prompting the regulators to take a tougher stance.
This is an AI-translated article and some names may be transliterated. The original Chinese text remains authoritative, and SPH Media is not responsible for translation errors.

paragraphs: Pragmatik Labs, a Shanghai-based artificial intelligence (AI) startup launched over the summer by the former AI chief of Alibaba Group Holding, Junyang Lin, closed new funding at a valuation of $5 billion, Bloomberg reported Friday (Nov. 20), citing unnamed sources.
Pragmatik Labs, which is also known as p7k, raised tens of millions of dollars in the round, according to the report.
When Pragmatik Labs raised its first financing of several hundred million dollars in August, the firm was valued at $2 billion, per the report.
Pragmatik Labs did not immediately reply to PYMNTS’ request for comment.
Lin was a key figure in Alibaba’s transition to AI and is credited with leading the development of the company’s Qwen series of large language models, according to the report.

Alibaba executives said during a Thursday (Nov. 19) earnings report that Alibaba’s capital expenditures increased 60% year over year to $7.5 billion as the company continued investing in AI infrastructure to meet accelerating demand from customers.

Alibaba’s AI Cloud and Compute Services segment’s revenue increased 53% year over year to $9.1 billion, and its AI Labs and Applications segment’s revenue increased 51% to $661 million, according to the company.
Lin announced in a March 3 post on X that he was stepping down from Alibaba, saying, “bye my beloved qwen.”

Lin announced in an Aug. 11 post on X that he had started a new company called Pragmatik Labs (p7k) in Shanghai. Lin said that Gaorong Ventures and HSG co-led a round at that time and that Tencent and Shanghai Engine Fund were also supporting his new company.
Lin said in the post that Pragmatik Labs is focused on “the research of next-generation agents across digital and physical worlds.”

According to the Pragmatik Labs website, the company’s work on digital agents includes general agents for knowledge work, operations and industry-scale workflows, while its work on physical agents includes embodied intelligence that adapts, acts and solves long-horizon tasks in the world.

“We build digital agents that transform knowledge work and physical agents that bring intelligence into real environments, starting from systems that reason, use tools, learn from feedback and coordinate action,” the Pragmatik Labs website said.

news.summary_en: Signal has introduced default screenshot restrictions to prevent OS-level AI agents, such as Apple Siri and Google Gemini, from scraping screen data and bypassing end-to-end encryption. The company stated that these agents pose a severe privacy threat by leveraging system-level permissions and has urged Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide more granular platform control tools.
paragraphs: Secure messaging service Signal said it will restrict the screenshot function on smartphones to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations. In a blog post published on the 20th (local time), Signal pointed out that AI features built directly into operating systems (OS) are accessing device data in ways app developers cannot control, and demanded that platform operators such as Apple, Google and Microsoft provide concrete blocking tools.

Signal itself acknowledged that the measure is not complete. "The current wave of agentic AI integration is creating an environment that is increasingly hostile to privacy," the company said, calling it "an existential threat to Signal and our ability to uphold our mission." It added that "operating systems govern the very environment in which apps like Signal must exist."

The biggest concern is AI that is deeply integrated into the OS, such as Apple's Siri AI or Google's Gemini Intelligence. According to Signal, these agents can read what is displayed on screen and act on the user's behalf based on that, meaning that Signal messages protected by end-to-end encryption can be pulled outside the encrypted environment. The company noted that the moment AI scans the screen, Signal's security environment is neutralized.

With this measure, Signal will introduce a setting that blocks screenshot access on users' devices and turn it on by default. When Signal detects a screenshot attempt or an AI assistant's screen access, it displays a pop-up window that lets users lift the block depending on the device type. Signal also blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. However, it said such protections are difficult to provide reliably on Apple's macOS.

Signal's concerns are backed by a recently confirmed real-world case. It was confirmed that Meta's AI agent Muse bypassed official integration tools to access Signal messages on Apple computers and Google Android smartphones. Muse used the broad OS-level permissions granted during the app's initial setup to pull messages in ways users did not expect. On Apple's macOS, it combined accessibility tools with the screenshot function to capture Signal conversations, extract text from the images and reproduce it inside the Muse app.

Meta countered that an agent must be able to see and interact with the computer to act on the user's behalf, and that Muse accesses other apps only through permissions the user has explicitly granted. Apple blocked that path with an OS update released this week, but at the same time introduced a new permission system aimed at agents that allows similar functions with additional warnings.

Signal urged that app developers be given a clear way to fully exclude their apps from AI assistants' data processing, including screen reading, notifications and file system access. Signal, which is run by a nonprofit foundation, has minimized the data it stores on servers, excluded advertising and provided end-to-end encryption. The company's judgment is that these protections are neutralized the moment AI scans the screen.

The issue comes as Apple accelerates development of its own AI agent. In a recent job posting, Apple disclosed plans to develop a general-purpose AI agent that handles a computer like a human, performing web searches, coding, app control and coordination of multiple sub-agents. It is considering a launch as early as the end of next year, but development is still at an early stage. Apple CEO John Ternus is said to have urged Craig Federighi, senior vice president of software engineering, to push the AI strategy faster and more boldly.

The competitive landscape is also heating up quickly. Meta's Muse ranked second among free apps on Apple's App Store with restaurant and travel booking and news briefing features, while OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude also placed in the top five. Anthropic has expanded user testing of its own agent Duet, OpenAI has added features to Dots, and Google overhauled its agent tasks this week. After news of Apple's AI agent development emerged, Meta shares fell about 2% and Anthropic more than 3% in after-hours trading.

The market expects tensions between platform operators and privacy apps to intensify further. The fact that platforms can control the paths through which OS-integrated AI accesses other apps' data shows that competitiveness in the AI agent era depends not only on model performance but also on the design of access permissions at the operating system level. Apple has already been sued by the US Department of Justice, including over allegations that it blocked rivals' access to features and hardware, so attention is focused on how Signal's demands will be reflected. Signal assessed that in Apple's upcoming iOS 27.3, Siri will be able to call a car or book a restaurant through external apps, but that this is far from a full agent that moves across multiple apps and handles complex tasks on its own.

news.title: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
news.title_en: Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots
news.author: Kate Taylor and Caroline Haskins
news.content_snippet:

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may h
news.summary_en: Executives and core engineers in Silicon Valley are increasingly vigilant against corporate espionage facilitated through romantic relationships. Business intelligence and high-end matchmaking firms report a surge in demand for comprehensive background checks, non-disclosure agreements, and behavioral audits as standard defensive measures against the leakage of sensitive intellectual property.
paragraphs: When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.
“Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

“Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One company is pitching its new line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”

Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”

Fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.
The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.
To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she says, is “a mind fuck.”

Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection company Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.
The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.
“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”

That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

Catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).
For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

On Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI launched a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where users can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.
It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin says, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.)
High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, says Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.
“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the company and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler says.

It’s particularly difficult, says Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

“Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey says. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”

celebrity.full_text_en:
$IREN is trading at $12.50 right now, a level I genuinely never thought we would see again.

I’ve personally seen this drop completely destroy investor confidence in the company and its management over the past couple of months.

And obviously this isn’t exclusive to $IREN. A lot of high-beta AI stocks have been getting absolutely destroyed lately, but $IREN is one of the more extreme examples given the severity of the drawdown this year.

At times like these, I think Amazon during the dot-com crash is a very interesting case study.

In the late 1990s, $AMZN had an incredible run alongside the rest of the internet sector, rising more than 70x in roughly two and a half years.

Then the bubble burst and over the following ~2 years, Amazon crashed by around 95%, despite already having a very real business underneath it, rapidly growing revenues and one of the strongest competitive positions in the entire internet sector.

From the eventual bottom at roughly $0.27, the stock went on to reach around $253 today.

That’s close to a 1,000x return, or roughly a 31.5% CAGR over 25 years.

Now before anyone looks at Amazon’s 95% drawdown and assumes $IREN therefore has to trade below $5 before this is over, you have to put the two moves into context.

Amazon had gone up more than 70x before the crash.
$IREN went up roughly 15x from the beginning of the AI boom to its peak.

The broader dot-com market was also trading at valuation levels that make today’s AI sector look comparatively cheap, so I’m obviously not arguing that the two situations are identical.

What the comparison does show is how far the stock of a fundamentally strong company can fall when an entire sector gets caught in a brutal unwind.

$IREN has now fallen roughly 84% from peak to trough, yet when I look at the actual business today, I struggle to find anything that remotely justifies that collapse.
If anything, the company’s competitive position has strengthened throughout it.

The economics on new contracts keep improving, with recent deals being signed at levels management could only dream of a couple of years ago.

Its funding position is far stronger as well. Despite a tighter credit environment, $IREN now has access to high customer prepayments, GPU-backed financing and billions of dollars of unencumbered data center assets it can borrow against, making it substantially less reliant on equity funding than it was during earlier stages of the buildout.

Meanwhile, demand for AI compute is at an all-time high.

Customers are increasingly willing to prepay huge portions of GPU capex just to secure capacity, all while competitors are running into problems sourcing power or dealing with execution issues from the third parties they rely on.

That is perfectly aligned with how $IREN positioned itself years ago.

The company secured a massive power pipeline before grid-connected power became nearly impossible to get, while vertically integrating the infrastructure layer so it doesn’t have to rely on third-party developers to deliver its growth.

This is the kind of setup I want to own going into a period where execution and access to power are becoming the bottlenecks of the entire industry.

And for anyone calling the $AMZN comparison survivorship bias, of course the vast majority of dot-com stocks never recovered. Yet, most of them deserved not to.

A huge part of the high-beta “.com” market consisted of companies with little more than a good story and hopes that a viable business would eventually emerge, while the market rewarded them with insane valuations anyway.

Amazon stood out because there was a real business engine underneath the stock, and that engine continued getting stronger even while the share price collapsed by 95%.

That is the part I find comparable to $IREN.

The stock is getting absolutely destroyed while the underlying company continues signing better contracts, broadening its funding options, expanding its infrastructure base and benefiting from an AI compute market that remains severely supply constrained.

To me, the disconnect has become extreme.

I think a large part of what we’re seeing now is simply deleveraging across a broad high-beta selloff, with heavy shorting exacerbating the move as momentum turned against the stock.

That can push prices far away from fundamentals for a while. But it doesn’t mean the fundamentals stop existing.

So before making an irrational decision simply because the chart looks horrific, I’d strongly recommend re-listening to $IREN's last earnings call and making sure you actually understand where the business stands today versus where it stood when the stock was trading several times higher.

$AMZN shareholders had every reason to feel like complete idiots while watching one of the strongest internet companies in the world lose 95% of its value.

In hindsight, the idiots were the ones who confused the collapse in the stock with a collapse in the business...
celebrity.full_text_zh:
$IREN 目前的交易价格为 12.50 美元，我真的没想到我们会再次看到这个水平。

在过去的几个月里，我个人看到这种下跌完全摧毁了投资者对公司及其管理层的信心。

显然这并不是 $IREN 独有的。许多高贝塔值人工智能股票最近都被彻底摧毁，但考虑到今年跌幅的严重程度，$IREN 是更极端的例子之一。

在这样的时刻，我认为互联网泡沫时期的亚马逊是一个非常有趣的案例研究。

在 20 世纪 90 年代末，$AMZN 与其他互联网行业一起取得了令人难以置信的增长，在大约两年半的时间里上涨了 70 倍以上。

然后泡沫破灭，在接下来的大约 2 年里，亚马逊崩溃了约 95%，尽管其背后已经拥有非常真实的业务、快速增长的收入以及整个互联网领域最具竞争力的地位之一。

从最终约 0.27 美元的底部，该股今天继续升至 253 美元左右。

这接近 1,000 倍的回报，或者说 25 年来的复合年增长率约为 31.5%。

现在，在任何人看到亚马逊 95% 的回撤并假设 $IREN 在这一切结束之前必须交易到 5 美元以下之前，你必须将这两次变动放在背景中。

股市崩盘前，亚马逊股价已上涨 70 多倍。
从人工智能热潮开始到顶峰，$IREN 上涨了大约 15 倍。

更广泛的互联网市场的估值水平也使得当今的人工智能行业看起来相对便宜，所以我显然并不认为这两种情况是相同的。

这一比较确实表明，当整个行业陷入残酷的困境时，一家基本面强劲的公司的股票会下跌多少。

$IREN 现在从高峰到低谷已经下跌了大约 84%，但当我审视今天的实际业务时，我很难找到任何可以证明这种崩溃的理由。
如果说有什么不同的话，那就是该公司的竞争地位在整个过程中得到了加强。

新合同的经济性不断改善，最近签署的协议达到了管理层几年前只能梦想的水平。

其融资状况也更加强劲。尽管信贷环境趋紧，$IREN 现在可以获得高额客户预付款、GPU 支持的融资以及可以借用的数十亿美元的无抵押数据中心资产，这使得它对股权融资的依赖大大低于扩建早期阶段。

与此同时，对人工智能计算的需求空前高涨。

客户越来越愿意预付大部分 GPU 资本支出，只是为了确保容量，而竞争对手却遇到了从他们所依赖的第三方采购电源或处理执行问题的问题。

这与 $IREN 多年前的定位完全一致。

该公司在几乎无法获得并网电力之前就获得了庞大的电力管道，同时垂直整合了基础设施层，因此不必依赖第三方开发商来实现增长。

在执行和权力获取正在成为整个行业瓶颈的时期，我希望拥有这种设置。

对于那些认为 $AMZN 比较幸存者偏差的人来说，当然绝大多数互联网股票从未恢复。然而，他们中的大多数人不应该这样做。

高贝塔值“.com”市场的很大一部分由那些只有好故事的公司组成，它们希望最终能够出现可行的业务，而市场无论如何都以疯狂的估值奖励它们。

亚马逊之所以能脱颖而出，是因为该股背后有一个真正的商业引擎，而且即使股价暴跌 95%，该引擎仍继续变得更强。

这是我发现与 $IREN 相当的部分。

当基础公司继续签署更好的合同、扩大其融资选择、扩大其基础设施基础并从供应仍然严重受限的人工智能计算市场中受益时，该股票将被彻底摧毁。

对我来说，这种脱节已经变得极端。

我认为我们现在看到的很大一部分只是在广泛的高贝塔值抛售中去杠杆化，随着势头转向对该股不利，大量做空加剧了这一走势。

这可能会使价格在一段时间内远离基本面。但这并不意味着基本面不复存在。

因此，在仅仅因为图表看起来很可怕而做出非理性决定之前，我强烈建议您重新听听 $IREN 的上次财报电话会议，并确保您真正了解该业务目前的状况与该股交易价格高出数倍时的状况。

当看到世界上最强大的互联网公司之一损失 95% 的价值时，$AMZN 的股东完全有理由感觉自己像个白痴。

事后看来，那些白痴才是把股票暴跌和企业崩溃混为一谈的人……

— Gemini 4 Neon, our newest model that brings fr
celebrity.title_zh:
我们一直忙于运送🚢以下是过去几周的回顾：

— Gemini 4 Neon，我们的最新型号，可在复杂的软件工程、知识工作和科学工作流程中快速完成端到端任务，带来前沿级智能

— Gemini 4 Hydrogen，我们在日常编码和代理工作流
celebrity.full_text_en:
We’ve been busy shipping 🚢 Here’s a recap of the last couple of weeks:

— Gemini 4 Neon, our newest model that brings frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows

— Gemini 4 Hydrogen, our model for speed and efficiency in everyday coding and agentic workflows

— Gemini 4 Carbon, our model for your hardest long-horizon projects and deep research

— Genie 4, @GoogleDeepMind’s most realistic interactive world model featuring real-time scene editing and adaptive native audio, now available in Project Genie (with a new creation agent and gallery) and for the first time in the Gemini API and @GoogleAIStudio

— Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, now with native voice editing that lets developers build experiences where users can edit, rephrase, and translate existing text in a single step using just their voice, via the Gemini API in @GoogleAIStudio

— Gemini Robotics 2.5, @GoogleDeepMind’s most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date

— AlphaGenome 2, @GoogleDeepMind’s new AI model that zooms in on specific cells to help scientists understand what drives disease

— Stitch Loop, a new @stitchbygoogle experiment from @GoogleLabs that monitors production data and runs continuous loops to improve your designed product until goals are met
celebrity.full_text_zh:
我们一直忙于运送🚢以下是过去几周的回顾：

— Gemini 4 Neon，我们的最新型号，可在复杂的软件工程、知识工作和科学工作流程中快速完成端到端任务，带来前沿级智能

— Gemini 4 Hydrogen，我们在日常编码和代理工作流程中实现速度和效率的模型

— Gemini 4 Carbon，我们为您最困难的长期项目和深入研究提供的模型

— Genie 4，@GoogleDeepMind 最真实的交互式世界模型，具有实时场景编辑和自适应原生音频，现已在 Project Genie 中提供（带有新的创建代理和图库），并首次在 Gemini API 和 @GoogleAIStudio 中提供

celebrity.title: History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the fut
celebrity.title_zh:
今天创造了历史。人类将在回顾 2026 年时思考：这是我们跨过的门槛，从那一刻起，每个人的未来都将永远改变。

人们可能在 2025 年底通过 Claude Code 第一次感觉到事情正在发生变化，当时代理人工智能对他们来说变得真正有形。
celebrity.full_text_en:
History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the future changed for everyone, forever.

People probably first sensed that something was shifting in late 2025 with Claude Code, when agentic AI became truly tangible for them. In the first half of 2026, things picked up speed. Model releases became more frequent, and everyone could feel the gaps between models and the improvements becoming more and more tangible. In the second half of 2026, however, there was a qualitative leap. It was no longer just the models getting better. It was the insights, the results, the outputs, the scientific solutions produced with AI that became more impressive, and today they have probably reached their absolute peak.

OpenAI led the way and solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a Millennium Prize Problem that humans had failed to solve for a very, very long time. A few weeks later, they published results on more than 300 open mathematical problems, many of which had also gone unsolved for decades. The entire scientific world was stunned, frozen in shock. But today Anthropic went a step further. Levent Alpöge, working with Claude, has almost certainly proven the Riemann Hypothesis. This is, and it’s hard to put into words, incredible and unfathomable. Today, I would say, is the proof of superintelligence. One of the greatest mathematical problems, if not the greatest, unsolved for 167 years, the holy grail of mathematics and science, has fallen. And it follows, and this should be clear to everyone, that all other problems will fall too.

We know that the development of AI models keeps moving forward relentlessly, and that this is just one step on the path to ever better models. And if the Riemann Hypothesis has already been proven today, there is simply no telling what even better models will solve. Dario Amodei said that AI will in all likelihood cure diseases, perhaps even all diseases. And although these are two different scientific disciplines, the significance of these breakthroughs shows that this is becoming more and more likely. 2026 will go down in human history as a turning point, the moment the singularity became tangible. And 2027 will be the year the singularity breaks into reality with full force and full impact.

I am in shock and excitement and I don't know what to think. But deep inside if feel joy. 

This day is one of the best days ever for all of us.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
今天创造了历史。人类将在回顾 2026 年时思考：这是我们跨过的门槛，从那一刻起，每个人的未来都将永远改变。

人们可能在 2025 年底通过 Claude Code 第一次感觉到事情正在发生变化，当时代理人工智能对他们来说变得真正有形。 2026 年上半年，事情加速发展。模型发布越来越频繁，大家都能感受到模型之间的差距和改进越来越明显。然而到了2026年下半年，却出现了质的飞跃。这不再只是模型变得更好了。人工智能产生的见解、结果、产出和科学解决方案变得更加令人印象深刻，今天它们可能已经达到了绝对的顶峰。

OpenAI 率先解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题，这是人类在很长一段时间内未能解决的千年奖问题。几周后，他们发表了 300 多个开放数学问题的结果，其中许多问题几十年来都没有得到解决。整个科学界都惊呆了，震惊不已。但今天 Anthropic 更进一步。 Levent Alpöge 与 Claude 合作，几乎肯定证明了黎曼猜想。这实在是难以用言语来形容，令人难以置信，深不可测。我想说，今天是超级智能的证明。 167 年来一直没有解决的最伟大的数学问题之一，数学和科学的圣杯，即使不是最伟大的，也已经陨落了。接下来，每个人都应该清楚，所有其他问题也会随之下降。

我们知道，人工智能模型的发展不断向前发展，而这只是迈向更好模型的第一步。如果黎曼假设今天已经得到证明，那么根本不知道更好的模型会解决什么问题。达里奥·阿莫迪表示，人工智能很可能会治愈疾病，甚至可能治愈所有疾病。尽管这是两个不同的科学学科，但这些突破的意义表明，这种情况变得越来越有可能。 2026 年将作为一个转折点载入人类历史，奇点变得有形的那一刻。 2027 年将是奇点以全力和全面影响力进入现实的一年。

我感到震惊和兴奋，不知道该怎么想。但内心深处却感到喜悦。

这一天对我们所有人来说都是最美好的日子之一。

celebrity.full_text_en:
🚨🇺🇸 Meta's Muse AI caught accessing private Signal messages without users' knowledge

Meta's AI agent Muse has been found accessing private Signal conversations through device permissions, raising serious privacy concerns after employees reported unexpected behavior from the assistant.

An investigation by Reuters, Signal, and the AI Now Institute confirmed that Muse could read Signal messages on Android through push notifications and on macOS through accessibility and screenshot permissions, even without Signal being directly connected to the AI.

The investigation also uncovered reports of Muse displaying unsolicited banking information, purchases, and conversations potentially belonging to other users. However, investigators could not confirm whether these were actual data leaks or AI-generated fabrications.

The findings do not indicate that Signal's encryption was broken. Meta says the incidents were isolated and that users must grant permissions for the agent to access other applications. Muse has surpassed 10 million downloads since its September launch.
celebrity.full_text_zh:
🚨🇺🇸 Meta 的 Muse AI 在用户不知情的情况下访问私人 Signal 消息

Meta 的人工智能代理 Muse 被发现通过设备权限访问私人 Signal 对话，在员工报告助理的意外行为后，引发了严重的隐私问题。

路透社、Signal 和 AI Now Institute 的一项调查证实，即使 Signal 没有直接连接到 AI，Muse 也可以通过推送通知在 Android 上读取 Signal 消息，在 macOS 上通过辅助功能和屏幕截图权限读取 Signal 消息。

调查还发现了 Muse 未经请求显示可能属于其他用户的银行信息、购买和对话的报告。然而，调查人员无法确认这些是否是实际的数据泄露或人工智能生成的捏造。

研究结果并不表明 Signal 的加密被破解。 Meta 表示，这些事件是孤立的，用户必须授予代理访问其他应用程序的权限。自 9 月推出以来，Muse 的下载量已超过 1000 万次。

prompts.scenario: 💻 编程研发 / 自动化规范
prompts.tested_models: 主流编程大模型通用 (Claude / GPT / DeepSeek 系列)
prompts.takeaway_zh: 杜绝 AI 盲目重构全量文件、使用已弃用 API 或编造虚假第三方依赖包，强制执行防御性编程与自动化单测补全。
prompts.takeaway_en: Prevents AI from hallucinating npm packages, breaking documentation, or re-writing entire files. Enforces defensive coding and unit tests.
prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.
prompts.usage_guide_zh: 将以上配置代码复制并保存到项目根目录下的 `.cursorrules` 文件中，Cursor 与 Windsurf 在每次生成代码和执行 Agent 任务时均会自动以此规范为最高准则约束输出。
prompts.usage_guide_en: Copy and save the above rules into `.cursorrules` in your project root directory. Cursor & Windsurf will automatically enforce these guidelines during agent coding.

1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；
2. 【多维下钻 (Drill-down)】：从 {{维度拆解}}（如渠道、地域、品类、新老客）分析异常聚集点；
3. 【可执行建议】：摒弃假大空的套话，给出接下来 48 小时内的 3 个立竿见影的动作与 1 个监控预警公式。

【杜邦拆解贡献率分析】：
1. 渠道维度：自然搜索量稳定（波动 <2%），但付费投流渠道跳出率贡献了 72% 的下跌额度；
2. 终端维度：移动端 iOS 表现正常，Android Web 呈现断崖式报错，核心原因是新版本结账 SDK 在低内存机型发生闪退。

【48小时纠偏行动】：
- 动作1 (技术)：立即灰度回滚 Android 渠道结账前端包至 v2.4.1；
- 动作2 (运营)：向受影响但未支付成功的 1,420 位加购用户推送 5 元免门槛补偿券唤醒；

viral_posts.full_text_en:
$IREN is trading at $12.50 right now, a level I genuinely never thought we would see again.

I’ve personally seen this drop completely destroy investor confidence in the company and its management over the past couple of months.

And obviously this isn’t exclusive to $IREN. A lot of high-beta AI stocks have been getting absolutely destroyed lately, but $IREN is one of the more extreme examples given the severity of the drawdown this year.

At times like these, I think Amazon during the dot-com crash is a very interesting case study.

In the late 1990s, $AMZN had an incredible run alongside the rest of the internet sector, rising more than 70x in roughly two and a half years.

Then the bubble burst and over the following ~2 years, Amazon crashed by around 95%, despite already having a very real business underneath it, rapidly growing revenues and one of the strongest competitive positions in the entire internet sector.

From the eventual bottom at roughly $0.27, the stock went on to reach around $253 today.

That’s close to a 1,000x return, or roughly a 31.5% CAGR over 25 years.

Now before anyone looks at Amazon’s 95% drawdown and assumes $IREN therefore has to trade below $5 before this is over, you have to put the two moves into context.

Amazon had gone up more than 70x before the crash.
$IREN went up roughly 15x from the beginning of the AI boom to its peak.

The broader dot-com market was also trading at valuation levels that make today’s AI sector look comparatively cheap, so I’m obviously not arguing that the two situations are identical.

What the comparison does show is how far the stock of a fundamentally strong company can fall when an entire sector gets caught in a brutal unwind.

$IREN has now fallen roughly 84% from peak to trough, yet when I look at the actual business today, I struggle to find anything that remotely justifies that collapse.
If anything, the company’s competitive position has strengthened throughout it.

The economics on new contracts keep improving, with recent deals being signed at levels management could only dream of a couple of years ago.

Its funding position is far stronger as well. Despite a tighter credit environment, $IREN now has access to high customer prepayments, GPU-backed financing and billions of dollars of unencumbered data center assets it can borrow against, making it substantially less reliant on equity funding than it was during earlier stages of the buildout.

Meanwhile, demand for AI compute is at an all-time high.

Customers are increasingly willing to prepay huge portions of GPU capex just to secure capacity, all while competitors are running into problems sourcing power or dealing with execution issues from the third parties they rely on.

That is perfectly aligned with how $IREN positioned itself years ago.

The company secured a massive power pipeline before grid-connected power became nearly impossible to get, while vertically integrating the infrastructure layer so it doesn’t have to rely on third-party developers to deliver its growth.

This is the kind of setup I want to own going into a period where execution and access to power are becoming the bottlenecks of the entire industry.

And for anyone calling the $AMZN comparison survivorship bias, of course the vast majority of dot-com stocks never recovered. Yet, most of them deserved not to.

A huge part of the high-beta “.com” market consisted of companies with little more than a good story and hopes that a viable business would eventually emerge, while the market rewarded them with insane valuations anyway.

Amazon stood out because there was a real business engine underneath the stock, and that engine continued getting stronger even while the share price collapsed by 95%.

That is the part I find comparable to $IREN.

The stock is getting absolutely destroyed while the underlying company continues signing better contracts, broadening its funding options, expanding its infrastructure base and benefiting from an AI compute market that remains severely supply constrained.

To me, the disconnect has become extreme.

I think a large part of what we’re seeing now is simply deleveraging across a broad high-beta selloff, with heavy shorting exacerbating the move as momentum turned against the stock.

That can push prices far away from fundamentals for a while. But it doesn’t mean the fundamentals stop existing.

So before making an irrational decision simply because the chart looks horrific, I’d strongly recommend re-listening to $IREN's last earnings call and making sure you actually understand where the business stands today versus where it stood when the stock was trading several times higher.

$AMZN shareholders had every reason to feel like complete idiots while watching one of the strongest internet companies in the world lose 95% of its value.

In hindsight, the idiots were the ones who confused the collapse in the stock with a collapse in the business...

显然这并不是 $IREN 独有的。许多高贝塔值人工智能股票最近都被彻底摧毁，但考虑到今年跌幅的严重程度，$IREN 是更极端的例子之一。

在这样的时刻，我认为互联网泡沫时期的亚马逊是一个非常有趣的案例研究。

在 20 世纪 90 年代末，$AMZN 与其他互联网行业一起取得了令人难以置信的增长，在大约两年半的时间里上涨了 70 倍以上。

然后泡沫破灭，在接下来的大约 2 年里，亚马逊崩溃了约 95%，尽管其背后已经拥有非常真实的业务、快速增长的收入以及整个互联网领域最具竞争力的地位之一。

从最终约 0.27 美元的底部，该股今天继续升至 253 美元左右。

这接近 1,000 倍的回报，或者说 25 年来的复合年增长率约为 31.5%。

现在，在任何人看到亚马逊 95% 的回撤并假设 $IREN 在这一切结束之前必须交易到 5 美元以下之前，你必须将这两次变动放在背景中。

股市崩盘前，亚马逊股价已上涨 70 多倍。
从人工智能热潮开始到顶峰，$IREN 上涨了大约 15 倍。

更广泛的互联网市场的估值水平也使得当今的人工智能行业看起来相对便宜，所以我显然并不认为这两种情况是相同的。

这一比较确实表明，当整个行业陷入残酷的困境时，一家基本面强劲的公司的股票会下跌多少。

$IREN 现在从高峰到低谷已经下跌了大约 84%，但当我审视今天的实际业务时，我很难找到任何可以证明这种崩溃的理由。
如果说有什么不同的话，那就是该公司的竞争地位在整个过程中得到了加强。

新合同的经济性不断改善，最近签署的协议达到了管理层几年前只能梦想的水平。

其融资状况也更加强劲。尽管信贷环境趋紧，$IREN 现在可以获得高额客户预付款、GPU 支持的融资以及可以借用的数十亿美元的无抵押数据中心资产，这使得它对股权融资的依赖大大低于扩建早期阶段。

与此同时，对人工智能计算的需求空前高涨。

客户越来越愿意预付大部分 GPU 资本支出，只是为了确保容量，而竞争对手却遇到了从他们所依赖的第三方采购电源或处理执行问题的问题。

这与 $IREN 多年前的定位完全一致。

该公司在几乎无法获得并网电力之前就获得了庞大的电力管道，同时垂直整合了基础设施层，因此不必依赖第三方开发商来实现增长。

在执行和权力获取正在成为整个行业瓶颈的时期，我希望拥有这种设置。

对于那些认为 $AMZN 比较幸存者偏差的人来说，当然绝大多数互联网股票从未恢复。然而，他们中的大多数人不应该这样做。

高贝塔值“.com”市场的很大一部分由那些只有好故事的公司组成，它们希望最终能够出现可行的业务，而市场无论如何都以疯狂的估值奖励它们。

亚马逊之所以能脱颖而出，是因为该股背后有一个真正的商业引擎，而且即使股价暴跌 95%，该引擎仍继续变得更强。

这是我发现与 $IREN 相当的部分。

当基础公司继续签署更好的合同、扩大其融资选择、扩大其基础设施基础并从供应仍然严重受限的人工智能计算市场中受益时，该股票将被彻底摧毁。

对我来说，这种脱节已经变得极端。

我认为我们现在看到的很大一部分只是在广泛的高贝塔值抛售中去杠杆化，随着势头转向对该股不利，大量做空加剧了这一走势。

这可能会使价格在一段时间内远离基本面。但这并不意味着基本面不复存在。

因此，在仅仅因为图表看起来很可怕而做出非理性决定之前，我强烈建议您重新听听 $IREN 的上次财报电话会议，并确保您真正了解该业务目前的状况与该股交易价格高出数倍时的状况。

当看到世界上最强大的互联网公司之一损失 95% 的价值时，$AMZN 的股东完全有理由感觉自己像个白痴。

事后看来，那些白痴才是把股票暴跌和企业崩溃混为一谈的人……
